To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
air seeding threshold varies between organs of mature sugar maple, and is lower in regions of the stem with higher ratios of primary to secondary xylems.
air seeding thresholds in A. saccharumar e higher in basal than distal regions of the tree, and are higher in primary xylems than in secondary xylem.

the air seeding thresholds of intervessel pit membranes in mature sugar maple ( Acer saccharium ) trees varied along the vertical axis, with distal organs (leaves and petioles) having lower air seeding thresholds than basal regions (trunk and roots).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial pattern of air-seeding thresholds in mature sugar maples.
the distribution of air seeding threshold in the stem of A. sacchrum and the factors influencing this spatial distribution.
the spatial pattern of air-seeding threshold in A. saccharumar and the factors that may be responsible for this pattern.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
P a is greater in the basal regions of A. saccharum, and this is due to the presence of wider secondary xylem conduicts, and not to the presence of smaller primary xylem cells.

the P a of primary and secondary xilem vessels are different, but the difference in P a is not related to vessel diameter, and is instead driven by differences in the amount of pit membrane exposed to the air.
the air seeding threshold of xylem conduicts is not constant throughout the tree, but varies according to the anatomical features of the vessel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of primary cell walls in primary xylems is the primary factor influencing the air-seeding threshold of xylem conductions.
air seeding thresholds are not uniform across all organs of a tree, but vary according to the relative proportions of primary and secondary xylary elements.
P a is not a simple function of vessel diameter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the air-seeding threshold is not a constant property of xylem conductions, but varies between regions of trees.
P a is not constant within the tree and varies with the anatomical structure of different regions of the stem.
the spatial distribution of air seeding threshold is not a simple function of vessel diameter and that primary xylem is an important component of the hydraulic architecture of trees.
